distinguishing_features: Passive re-machined nozzle-inlet orifice/annular-core geometry that creates a localized thermal lag at the crack-initiation site.
Local decoupling of nozzle thermal response from the vessel global cycle while leaving the global pressure/temperature operating envelope unchanged.
Design/acceptance criterion based on thermal time constants of injected flow mass versus nozzle wall rather than inferred EGT/thermal-stress limits and active derating.
Hardware configuration change rather than firmware/control-logic duty capping or new monitoring sensors.
parsed.objective_technical_problem: How to reduce cyclic thermal strain at a pressure-vessel nozzle crack-initiation site during vessel thermal transients while preserving the vessel's global operating duty and avoiding new monitoring hardware or reactive repair.
parsed.viable_reason: A high-velocity flowing slug has short residence time and increased heat-transfer coefficient, so it cannot supply the claimed lumped thermal inertia, while the orifice array adds turbulence and stress concentrators and the solid-conduction time-constant calculation does not support the asserted attenuation.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: Closest art 2 reduces the same thermal-fatigue driver by inference and active derating, and it provides no teaching or motivation to re-machine a nozzle with a passive thermal-inertia/orifice flow path, so the distinguishing mechanism is not a routine parameter change.
